section_title: What limit is placed on the ruler who opposes God?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 23 This is what he said: ‘The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will appear on the earth, different from all the other kingdoms, and it will devour the whole earth, trample it down, and crush it. 24 And the ten horns are ten kings who will rise from this kingdom. After them another king, different from the earlier ones, will rise and subdue three kings. 25 He will speak out against the Most High and oppress the saints of the Most High, intending to change the appointed times and laws; and the saints will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.

26 But the court will convene, and his dominion will be taken away and completely destroyed forever. 27 Then the sovereignty, dominion, and greatness of the kingdoms under all of heaven will be given to the people, the saints of the Most High. His kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom, and all rulers will serve and obey Him.’ 28 Thus ends the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts troubled me greatly, and my face turned pale. But I kept the matter to myself.”

context_lines: The explanation identifies the fourth beast as a kingdom and the ten horns as kings. Another king rises after them, puts down three, speaks against the Most High and oppresses His saints. He intends to change the appointed times and laws.

The saints are given into his power for a time, times and half a time. Then the court sits, his dominion is taken away, and the greatness of the kingdoms under heaven is given to the people of the Most High. His kingdom endures, and rulers serve and obey Him.

Daniel closes still pale and troubled, keeping the matter to himself. The vision offers a firm outcome without making the intervening suffering easy. Its final authority belongs to God’s court, and its final kingdom belongs to Him.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/daniel/7.htm) and [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/daniel/7.htm) connect the persecuting ruler with papal power in their readings. [Gaebelein](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gaebelein/daniel/7.htm) expects a future ruler within a revived Roman Empire. The [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/daniel/7) understand the oppression and changes to worship in relation to Antiochus IV.

The three-and-a-half period is commonly understood as a limited period of persecution. Readings differ over its historical setting and how it relates to later prophecy. The explanation itself ends with the removal of the oppressor and the enduring kingdom of God.
